title: Why A Simple Pause Is A Powerful Classroom Management Strategy m-management-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies a common teaching flaw: stringing sentences together without pause, which makes a teacher uninteresting and hard to follow. He proposes deliberate, sometimes lengthy pauses as a simple fix with outsized benefits. Pauses help students predict what comes next, build suspense and curiosity, add depth and drama to delivery, discourage boredom-driven misbehavior, give teachers a moment to check understanding, and help students retain information in digestible chunks. He acknowledges that pausing can feel uncomfortable at first but becomes a natural, powerful habit with practice. The article frames this small technique as part of the broader truth that simple, consistently applied practices are what make great teaching.
points: Speaking without pauses, filling gaps with filler words, makes teachers uninteresting and pushes students toward daydreaming and misbehavior.
Strategic pauses build anticipation and suspense, making even mundane information feel worth listening to.
Pauses give teachers a moment to check for understanding and make eye contact before continuing.
Breaking directions and content into pause-separated chunks helps students retain information better.
Pausing may feel uncomfortable at first but becomes a powerful, natural habit that increases teacher confidence and effectiveness.
quotes: Bridging phrases together without allowing your students time to absorb them makes you uninteresting and difficult to follow.
It causes students to turn their attention away from you and toward the daydreams, distractions, and misbehavior opportunities around them.
Anticipating answers and outcomes improves learning, and when you pause, your students will instinctively predict what you’re going to say next.
When used strategically, a pause creates suspense and curiosity in the listener, causing them to sit up straighter and lean in closer.
Speaking without intentional pausing sounds like droning to students, who are quick to lose interest, grow bored, and misbehave.
An occasional pause, if for only a second or two, breaks ideas, theories, and directives into chunks, allowing them to sink in before your students are rushed along to the next thing.
